paragraphs: Geviha ben Pesisa, a great sage in the days of Shimon the Righteous. In the sabbatical year he defeated the people of Africa, the descendants of Ishmael, the descendants of Keturah, and the Egyptians before Alexander of Macedon (see part 1, year 3448). Because of his advanced age, his back was bent. In chapter Chelek, 91, he gave a reason for the resurrection of the dead: “What did not exist came into being; is it not all the more so with what already existed?” In Bereshit Rabbah, Chayyei Sarah, chapter 61: Gevia ben Kosem; likewise in the Arukh, entry gevia. Some say that Geviha was tall and upright and was a guard of the Temple, and that Gevia ben Kosem is the name of a sage (Yuchasin, in the order of the generations, under Shimon the Righteous). Shalshelet HaKabbalah, folio 102: “Canaanites came before the king to demand the land of Canaan that Joshua conquered; Ishmaelites came to contest the birthright; and Egyptians came to demand the spoil and booty that the children of Israel took out of Egypt. Geviha ben Pesisa, an ordinary priest, answered them all, and they fled from before the king.” End of quotation. I do not know where he obtained the claim that he was an ordinary priest. Perhaps he derived it from what is stated there in Chelek, that Geviha said to the sages, “I shall go; if they defeat me, say, ‘You defeated an ordinary man among us.’” According to the aforementioned Yuchasin, that he was a guard of the Temple, there is no proof that he was a priest, for the priests guard in three places and the Levites in twenty-one places, as stated at the beginning of Middot.
